summary: Specifies rules for translating YANG data models into the Document Schema Definition Languages (DSDL), a family of XML schema languages, so NETCONF content can be validated. The target languages include RELAX NG and Schematron. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A translator that turns one way of describing network data into another that existing checking tools understand, so data can be checked for mistakes.

questions: what is yang to dsdl mapping
subtitle: Rules for turning YANG data models into standard XML schemas so NETCONF data can be checked automatically.

tldr.problem: NETCONF carries its data as XML, and YANG describes that data, but YANG alone gave no standard way to check XML documents with off-the-shelf validators.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC maps YANG modules in two steps: first to a single annotated RELAX NG 'hybrid schema', then to a coordinated set of RELAX NG, Schematron and DSRL schemas for one chosen kind of document.
tldr.outcome: Validators can check grammar and data types, fill in defaults, and then check semantic constraints. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 7952.

today: RFC 6110 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 7952. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why YANG Needs a Mapping to Schemas
sections.content:
NETCONF is a configuration management protocol whose messages are encoded in XML. Its base specification, RFC 4741, defines the protocol bindings and an XML container syntax, but not a language for modelling the configuration and state data it carries. The NETMOD Working Group designed YANG (RFC 6020) to fill that gap, with a focus on readability and ease of use.

Because NETCONF content is XML, it is natural to express its constraints with standard XML schema languages. The working group chose the Document Schema Definition Languages (DSDL, ISO/IEC 19757). This RFC specifies how to translate YANG modules into DSDL schemas, and how to use the results to validate XML documents such as datastore contents and NETCONF messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Network devices are set up using a special kind of form. This RFC explains how to turn the form's rules into a checklist that ordinary checking programs can use.

sections.title: The Three DSDL Languages
sections.content:
DSDL follows a principle of small languages: each part is a stand-alone schema language with a narrow focus, and they are used together. The mapping uses three of them.

  • RELAX NG (Part 2) checks grammar and the structure and contents of XML documents. It deliberately avoids defining default values, and it uses the W3C XML Schema datatypes as its base type library. It has an XML syntax and a compact syntax; this RFC uses the XML syntax only.
  • Schematron (Part 3) is rule based. Each rule has a context (an XPath expression), an assert or report condition, and a human-readable message. It suits arbitrary conditions across different parts of a document.
  • DSRL (Part 8) is allowed to modify the XML information set. The mapping uses it to insert default content that is missing from the validated document.

The mapping also uses three sets of annotations added to RELAX NG schemas: Dublin Core metadata, the RELAX NG DTD compatibility annotation a:documentation for YANG 'description' and 'reference' texts, and NETMOD-specific annotations in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netmod:dsdl-annotations:1 (prefix nma).
sections.plainLanguage: Think of three helpers: one checks that the sentence is built correctly, one checks that it makes sense, and one fills in blanks you left out.

sections.title: The Two-Step Mapping
sections.content:
The mapping is split into two steps so the final schemas stay readable. In step one, one or more YANG modules are transformed into the hybrid schema, a single RELAX NG schema that describes the data tree, RPC operations and notifications. Constraints RELAX NG cannot express, such as list keys and 'must' statements, plus documentation, are recorded as foreign-namespace annotations. The hybrid schema is a near-complete equivalent of the YANG input, but it cannot be used for validation directly.

In step two, the hybrid schema is transformed into a coordinated set of three schemas for one specific document type and context: a RELAX NG schema for grammar and data types, a Schematron schema for other constraints such as list-key uniqueness and user-written rules, and a DSRL schema for default contents.

An implementation MUST accept one or more valid YANG modules as input, because several modules may be negotiated in one NETCONF session. The generated schemas are meant to be made on demand for a particular purpose and to have a short life, not to be maintained alongside the YANG modules.
sections.plainLanguage: First you write everything down in one big notebook. Then, for each job, you copy out just the pages you need into three smaller checklists.

sections.title: The Hybrid Schema and Design Choices
sections.content:
Each input YANG module becomes exactly one embedded grammar inside the hybrid schema. Marker elements in the nma namespace separate configuration and state data, RPC operations and notifications. The hybrid schema is not even a valid RELAX NG schema, since it holds several schemas set apart by these markers.

The RFC discusses several design decisions. For modularity, YANG imports only definitions while RELAX NG includes whole schema trees, so the final RELAX NG output is split into two files: one for global definitions mapped from top-level groupings (which MUST NOT set an @ns attribute) and one with the data trees, each in its own embedded grammar that declares its namespace with @ns. Submodules are not mapped separately and are treated as if their text were in the main module.

For granularity, YANG modules tend to be nested ('Russian Doll' style) while RELAX NG schemas tend to be flatter, so the mapping keeps the granularity of the original: groupings and derived types usually become named patterns. For namespaces, the root grammar MUST declare prefixes for all namespaces used, and Schematron requires each namespace in an sch:ns element.
sections.plainLanguage: Each YANG file gets its own chapter in the notebook, with tabs to mark which pages are settings, which are commands and which are announcements.

sections.title: Mapping YANG Constructs
sections.content:
Section 9 explains the main principles of step one, and Section 10 gives rules for each YANG statement, from 'anyxml' to 'yin-element'. Several points stand out.

Optional, mandatory and implicit nodes. A leaf, anyxml or choice node is mandatory if it has mandatory true;, and a list key leaf is mandatory too. A list or leaf-list is mandatory if its 'min-elements' is greater than zero. A container without 'presence' is mandatory if any child is mandatory. All other nodes are optional and get an rng:optional wrapper. An implicit node is one that can be added to or dropped from the data tree without changing its meaning, such as a leaf with a default value; these are marked @nma:default or @nma:implicit.

Groupings and typedefs become RELAX NG named patterns. Their names are mangled by prefixing the module name and two underscores, adding a leading underscore for groupings, and appending __rpc when a grouping needs a fixed element order for RPC parameters. A 'uses' statement with 'refine' or 'augment' is expanded in place rather than mapped to a pattern reference. A derived type used without restrictions maps to a pattern reference, while one with restrictions is expanded to its ancestor built-in type with the combined facets.
sections.plainLanguage: Every kind of YANG building block has a matching RELAX NG block. Reusable pieces get unique name tags so they do not get mixed up, and pieces that get tweaked are copied out in full.

sections.title: Validating NETCONF Content
sections.content:
To validate an XML instance document such as a datastore or a NETCONF message, the generated schemas are applied in three steps.

  1. The RELAX NG schema checks grammar and data types.
  2. The DSRL schema fills in default leaf values and adds their ancestor containers where needed. This step changes the information set of the document. It must come before the next step because YANG (RFC 6020) requires the data tree for XPath evaluation to already have all defaults filled in.
  3. The Schematron schema checks semantic constraints.

The second mapping step needs to know which kind of document is being validated, for example a datastore, a reply to nc:get or nc:get-config, other RPC requests and replies, or a notification. It extracts the matching part of the hybrid schema, wraps it in the right NETCONF elements, and maps annotations to Schematron and DSRL rules. For a get-config reply, elements marked @nma:config with the value false are removed. Section 12 gives the mapping for each annotation, and Appendix C shows a full example with a DHCP data model.
sections.plainLanguage: You first check the spelling and grammar, then fill in the blanks you left, and last check that everything makes sense together.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The RFC says the mapping procedure itself has no security impact on the Internet. The DSDL schemas it produces can validate NETCONF messages or whole datastores, adding checks beyond those done by NETCONF servers and clients that support YANG. How strict the validation is comes directly from the source YANG modules.

For IANA, the document requests two registrations in the IETF XML registry: the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netmod:dsdl-annotations:1 and the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netmod:xpath-extensions:1.
sections.plainLanguage: Checking the rules does not open any new doors for bad guys. It just gives one more way to catch mistakes.
